questions.q: For the annual day, Mrs Sharma buys ribbon to make badge sets. Each set needs 2 1/2 m of ribbon and she makes 9 sets. (a) How many metres of ribbon does she need? (b) The ribbon costs ₹16 per metre. Find the total cost. (c) She has ₹400. How many more sets can she make with the money left?
questions.a: (a) 9 × 5/2 = 45/2 = 22 1/2 m. (b) 45/2 × 16 = ₹360. (c) Money left = ₹40. One more set needs 5/2 × 16 = ₹40, so exactly 1 more set.
s: Part (c): finds ₹40 left and 1 more set

questions.q: A security guard at a railway yard walks 1 1/2 km on every round. How far has he walked after 7 rounds?
Which of the following is 3 × 2/7 written as repeated addition?
(a) Write 2 1/3 as an improper fraction. (b) Mangoes cost ₹18 per kg. Find the cost of 2 1/3 kg.
s: Part (a): converts the mixed fraction to 7/3
Part (b): divides 18 by 3 and multiplies by 7 to get ₹42

questions.q: Following the book's method, how is 3/8 × 40 found?
questions.a: Divide 40 by 8 to get 5, then multiply 5 by 3
o: Divide 40 by 8 to get 5, then multiply 5 by 3
Divide 40 by 3, then multiply the result by 8
Multiply 40 by 8, then divide the result by 3
Add 3 and 8, then multiply the sum by 40

questions.q: Two methods for 7/10 × 40: Method A multiplies 7 × 40 = 280 and then divides by 10. Method B divides 40 by 10 and then multiplies by 7. (a) Do both give the same answer? State it. (b) Which method keeps the numbers smaller, and why? (c) Use Method B on 5/12 × 18. What do you notice about the first step, and what is the answer?
questions.a: (a) Yes, both give 28. (b) Method B, because 40 ÷ 10 = 4 first, so the second step is 7 × 4. (c) 18 ÷ 12 = 3/2 is a fraction, not a whole number; then 5 × 3/2 = 15/2 = 7 1/2.
s: Part (b): picks Method B with the reason that the division comes out exact and small

questions.q: Gauri drinks 3/4 litre of buttermilk every day. (a) How much does she drink in a week? (b) How much in April (30 days)? (c) Will a 20-litre can last her through April?
questions.a: (a) 7 × 3/4 = 21/4 = 5 1/4 litres. (b) 30 × 3/4 = 45/2 = 22 1/2 litres. (c) No, 22 1/2 litres is more than 20 litres.
s: Part (c): compares with 20 litres and says no

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
Statement 1: 7/12 × 3 can be found by dividing 3 by 12 and then multiplying the result by 7.
Statement 2: 5 × 2/9 = 10/45.
Statement 3: 1 1/4 × 8 = 10.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q: A pump fills 2/9 of a water tank in one hour. (a) What part of the tank does it fill in 4 hours? (b) How many full tanks does it fill in 9 hours?
questions.a: (a) 4 × 2/9 = 8/9 of the tank. (b) 9 × 2/9 = 2 full tanks.
s: Part (b): multiplies 9 by 2/9 to get 2 tanks

questions.q:
On sports day at a Jaipur school, each of the 18 runners in the 400 m race is to be given 3/4 litre of water at the finish line. The teacher has one 12-litre drum of water. A shopkeeper next door can sell a 2-litre can for ₹30. The teacher is thinking of two plans: Plan X reduces each runner's share to 2/3 litre; Plan Y keeps 3/4 litre each and buys the extra can.
(a) How many litres do the runners need in all at 3/4 litre each?
(b) By how many litres is the drum short?
(c) How many litres do the runners need under Plan X?
(d) Which plan would you advise, and why? Use your answers.
questions.a: (a) 18 × 3/4 = 27/2 = 13 1/2 L. (b) 13 1/2 - 12 = 1 1/2 L short. (c) 18 × 2/3 = 12 L, exactly the drum. (d) Either is defensible: Plan X costs nothing and uses the drum exactly but leaves no spare water and gives smaller shares; Plan Y costs ₹30 but the 2 L can covers the 1 1/2 L shortfall with 1/2 L spare. Recommending Plan Y with that reason (or X with its reason) earns the mark.
s: Part (d): picks a plan and justifies it using 1 1/2 L shortfall, 12 L exact, or ₹30 cost

questions.q:
Mr Joseph, a tailor in Kochi, must stitch school bags. Each bag uses 2 1/4 m of canvas. Canvas sold by length costs ₹40 per metre. A dealer also sells a whole roll of 40 m for ₹1,500. Mr Joseph first wants to stitch 16 bags.
(a) How many metres of canvas do 16 bags need?
(b) What does that cloth cost if bought by the metre?
(c) How much more does the roll cost than your answer to (b), and how much canvas is then left over?
(d) A customer asks for one more bag, making 17. Which way of buying is cheaper for 17 bags, by how much?
questions.a: (a) 16 × 9/4 = 36 m. (b) 36 × 40 = ₹1,440. (c) ₹1,500 - ₹1,440 = ₹60 more; 40 - 36 = 4 m left over. (d) 17 bags need 153/4 = 38 1/4 m, which costs 153/4 × 40 = ₹1,530 by the metre; the roll at ₹1,500 is cheaper by ₹30.
s: Part (c): ₹60 more and 4 m left over
Part (d): ₹1,530 by the metre, roll cheaper by ₹30

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 3/7 × 4 = 12/7.
Reason (R): The product 3/7 × 4 means dividing 4 into 7 equal parts and taking 3 of those parts.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Write 5 × 3/8 as a repeated addition, and hence as one fraction and as a mixed fraction.
s: Writes five terms of 3/8 added together

questions.q: Make up a short real-life story, with a unit, whose answer is 6 × 5/8. Then work out the answer.
questions.a: Sample: A beekeeper fills 6 jars with 5/8 kg of honey each. Honey = 6 × 5/8 = 30/8 = 15/4 = 3 3/4 kg.
s: Gives a story with 6 equal groups of 5/8 of a unit
States the answer with its unit as 3 3/4 kg

questions.q:
Match each product in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. 5 × 2/3   2. 3/4 × 6   3. 1 1/2 × 4   4. 2/9 × 3
Column II: A. 6   B. 2/3   C. 9/2   D. 10/3
What is 1/5 × 3?
A tailor uses 3/4 m of cloth for one school apron. (a) How much cloth do 5 aprons need? (b) He has 4 m. Is that enough, and how much is left over or short?
questions.a: (a) 5 × 3/4 = 15/4 = 3 3/4 m. (b) Yes, 4 m is more than 3 3/4 m, so 1/4 m is left over.
s: Part (b): compares with 4 m and finds 1/4 m left

questions.q: (a) Use the divide-then-multiply method to find 9/4 × 6. (b) Write the answer as a mixed fraction.
s: Part (a): divides 6 by 4 and multiplies the result by 9 to get 27/2

questions.q: A school cook uses 3/4 kg of rice to fill one big pot at the Onam feast. How much rice does she need for 6 such pots?

Kabir says, '5/6 × 12 can be found either by adding 5/6 twelve times or by dividing 12 by 6 and multiplying by 5, and both ways give the same number.' Do you agree? Show both ways and say which is quicker.
questions.a: Yes. Adding 5/6 twelve times gives 60/6 = 10. Dividing 12 by 6 gives 2 and 2 × 5 = 10. Both give 10, but the second is quicker because it needs one division and one multiplication instead of twelve additions.
s: Gives the verdict that Kabir is right
Says which method is quicker, with the reason

questions.q: A unit square is cut into 5 rows and 6 columns, which is the picture for 4/6 × 3/5. (a) How many of the 30 small parts are shaded? (b) Write the product in lowest form.
s: Part (a): 12 parts shaded out of 30, giving 12/30

questions.q: Reena draws a unit square with 3 rows and 5 columns and shades 2 of the small parts lying in one row. What fraction of the whole square is shaded?

Aarti plans two herb beds in the school garden. The Tulsi bed is 3/5 m long and 5/6 m wide. The Mint bed is 2/3 m long and 4/5 m wide. Garden soil costs ₹90 per square metre, and she has been given ₹90 for soil.
(a) Find the area of the Tulsi bed.
(b) Find the area of the Mint bed.
(c) What does the soil cost for each bed?
(d) Can she fill both beds with her ₹90? Suggest what she should do and why.
questions.a: (a) 3/5 × 5/6 = 1/2 sq m. (b) 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15 sq m. (c) Tulsi 1/2 × 90 = ₹45; Mint 8/15 × 90 = ₹48. (d) Both need ₹93, which is ₹3 more than ₹90. She can fill one bed fully and the other nearly, or ask for ₹3 more; any choice justified with ₹93 > ₹90.
s: Part (d): sees ₹93 is above ₹90 and recommends a justified plan

questions.q: In the book's unit-square method, the number of rows equals the denominator of which fraction?
questions.a: The multiplicand

questions.q: (a) A unit square is divided into 7 rows and 9 columns. How many equal parts does it have? (b) Use this to write 1/7 × 1/9 as a single fraction.
s: Part (a): multiplies rows and columns to get 63
Part (b): writes one part of 63 as 1/63

questions.q: Meenakshi draws a rectangular rangoli 3/4 m long and 1/2 m wide on the school floor. (a) Find its area. (b) She colours 2/3 of the rangoli red. What area is red? (c) The red powder costs ₹80 per square metre. What does the red colour cost?
A rectangular herb bed is 2/3 m long and 4/5 m wide. (a) Find its area. (b) Is the area more or less than 1 square metre? Give a reason from the sides.
questions.a: (a) 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15 square metre. (b) Less than 1 square metre, because 8/15 is less than 1 and each side is shorter than 1 m.
s: Part (b): says less than 1 with a reason

questions.q: Rectangle A has sides 2/5 m and 3/4 m. Rectangle B has sides 3/10 m and 7/8 m. (a) Find the area of each. (b) Which area is bigger and by how much? (c) B has the longer side, yet its area is smaller. Explain how that can happen.
questions.a: (a) A = 3/10 = 24/80, B = 21/80. (b) A is bigger by 3/80 sq m. (c) The area depends on both sides: B's longer side 7/8 is matched with a much shorter side 3/10 (smaller than A's 2/5), so the product is smaller.
s: Part (c): says area depends on both sides and compares the shorter sides 3/10 and 2/5

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 1/6 × 1/7 = 1/42.
Reason (R): The product 1/6 × 1/7 is smaller than both 1/6 and 1/7.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
A farmer in Punjab owns a rectangular field 3/4 km long and 2/3 km wide. She grows sugarcane on a rectangle 1/2 km by 1/3 km and wheat on a rectangle 1/4 km by 2/3 km. The rest lies fallow. A neighbour offers to lease the fallow part for ₹6 lakh per square km per year. Growing millets there would give her ₹1,40,000 but cost ₹30,000 for seed and labour.
(a) Find the area of the whole field.
(b) Find the areas under sugarcane and wheat.
(c) What area is fallow?
(d) Should she lease the fallow part or grow millets? Use the money for each.
questions.a: (a) 3/4 × 2/3 = 1/2 sq km. (b) Sugarcane 1/6 sq km, wheat 1/6 sq km. (c) 1/2 - 1/6 - 1/6 = 1/6 sq km. (d) Lease: 1/6 × 6 lakh = ₹1,00,000. Millets: ₹1,40,000 - ₹30,000 = ₹1,10,000. Millets give ₹10,000 more but carry crop risk; leasing is safe. Either choice backed by these figures earns the mark.
s: Part (d): compares ₹1,00,000 with ₹1,10,000 and decides with a reason

questions.q: To find 1/4 × 1/6 with a unit square, into how many equal parts is the whole divided?
Rohan wrote 1/5 × 1/8 = 1/13. (a) What did he do wrongly? (b) Give the correct product.
questions.a: (a) He added the denominators 5 + 8 instead of multiplying them. (b) 1/40.
s: Part (a): names the error of adding the denominators

questions.q: A farmer's plot is 5/8 km long and 4/5 km wide. (a) Find its area in lowest form. (b) Is the area less than 1/2 square km? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 5/8 × 4/5 = 20/40 = 1/2 square km. (b) No, it is exactly 1/2 square km, neither less nor more.
s: Compares with 1/2 and says it is equal, not less

questions.q: What is the area of a rectangle whose sides are 1/3 unit and 1/7 unit?
questions.a: 1/21 square unit

questions.q: A rectangular rangoli tile is 1/2 m long and 1/5 m wide. What is its area?
questions.a: 1/10 square metre

questions.q: To find 1/15 × 1/20 a unit square is cut into equal parts in both directions. (a) How many equal parts does it have? (b) Use this to find 7/15 × 1/20.
Which of these is the value of 1/9 × 1/15?

Consider the statements.
Statement 1: 1/4 × 1/5 = 1/20.
Statement 2: A rectangle with sides 1/2 unit and 1/3 unit has area 1/6 square unit.
Statement 3: To find 1/b × 1/d, the unit square is always divided into b + d equal parts.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q: Tarun says, 'A rectangle with sides 1/4 m and 1/5 m has an area of 1/20 square metre, so exactly 20 such rectangles fit in a square of side 1 m.' Do you agree? Explain with the unit square.
questions.a: Yes. Cutting the unit square into 4 equal strips one way and 5 the other gives 4 × 5 = 20 equal parts. Each part is a rectangle of sides 1/4 and 1/5 and has area 1/20, so 20 of them fill the unit square exactly.
s: Gives the verdict that Tarun is right
Shows the unit square has 4 × 5 = 20 equal parts
Says each part has area 1/20 so 20 fill the square

questions.q: Show that a rectangle with sides 1/2 m and 1/3 m cannot have an area of 5/6 square metre.
questions.a: Area = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6 square metre, not 5/6. Also 5/6 is greater than the side 1/2, but the area of a rectangle with both sides below 1 is smaller than each side (1/6 is less than 1/2 and 1/3), so 5/6 is impossible.
s: Notes 5/6 is greater than the side 1/2
Concludes the area is smaller than each side, so 5/6 is impossible

questions.q: (a) Find 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4. (b) Multiply the result by 4/5 as well. What do you notice about the two answers?
questions.a: (a) 1/4. (b) 1/5. Each answer is 1 over the last denominator.
s: Part (b): 1/5 and notes the pattern of 1 over the last denominator

questions.q:
Match each product in Column I with its lowest form in Column II.
Column I: 1. 15/16 × 8/25   2. 9/14 × 7/12   3. 4 × 5/12   4. 6/35 × 10/21
Column II: A. 4/49   B. 5/3   C. 3/10   D. 3/8
A tailoring machine finishes 5/6 of a shirt in one hour. What part of a shirt does it finish in 3/4 of an hour?
A rectangular poster is 5/12 m long and 9/10 m wide. (a) Find its area in lowest form. (b) A second poster is 5/12 m long and 1 m wide. Which poster has the larger area, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 5/12 × 9/10 = 3/8 sq m. (b) The second poster has area 5/12 = 10/24 sq m against 9/24, so it is larger by 1/24 sq m.
s: Part (b): second poster larger by 1/24 square metre

questions.q: (a) Multiply 7/9 × 3/14 after cancelling common factors. (b) Name the common factors you cancelled.
questions.a: (a) 1/6. (b) 7 (between 7 and 14) and 3 (between 3 and 9).
s: Part (b): names the factors 7 and 3 cancelled across numerator and denominator

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In 2/3 × 4/9 the denominators 3 and 9 can be cancelled by 3.
Reason (R): A fraction keeps its value when its numerator and denominator are divided by the same common factor.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
In a school cycling activity, Rani rides at 14/5 km per hour for 5/12 hour. Imran rides at 9/4 km per hour for 8/9 hour. The teacher will give the flag to the rider who covers the greater distance. Later Rani asks to ride for 5/6 hour instead of 5/12 hour.
(a) How far does Rani ride?
(b) How far does Imran ride?
(c) By how much does one beat the other?
(d) If Rani rides 5/6 hour, how far does she go? Should the teacher allow the change? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 14/5 × 5/12 = 7/6 km. (b) 9/4 × 8/9 = 2 km. (c) Imran by 2 - 7/6 = 5/6 km. (d) 14/5 × 5/6 = 7/3 = 2 1/3 km, more than Imran's 2 km. Allowing it gives Rani exactly double the time so the contest is not fair; allowing it for both is the fair option. Any reason using these figures earns the mark.
s: Part (d): 7/3 km and a justified decision

questions.q: According to Brahmagupta's formula, a/b × c/d equals which of the following?
(a) Write 8 as a fraction and use Brahmagupta's formula to find 8 × 3/5. (b) Write the answer as a mixed fraction.
Kiran multiplies 21/20 × 8/35 by cancelling common factors first. What should her final answer be?
In a school library, 3/5 of the books are fiction and 5/12 of the fiction books are in Hindi. (a) What fraction of all books are Hindi fiction? (b) How many are these if the library has 960 books?
Neha says, 'When multiplying fractions I may cancel any two numbers that have a common factor.' Is she right? Test her idea on 6/7 × 4/9, which equals 8/21.
questions.a: Only partly. Cancelling a numerator with a denominator is allowed. But cancelling the two numerators 6 and 4 by 2 gives 3/7 × 2/9 = 2/21, which is not 8/21. So she may cancel only a numerator with a denominator.
s: Gives the verdict that she is right only partly
Shows that cancelling 6 and 4 gives 2/21, not 8/21
States the rule: cancel only a numerator with a denominator

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
Statement 1: To multiply 3/4 and 5/7 we add the numerators and add the denominators.
Statement 2: A whole number n can be written as n/1 and used in Brahmagupta's formula.
Statement 3: 35/12 × 18/25 = 21/10 after cancelling common factors.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q: Write two proper fractions, one with denominator 8 and the other with denominator 9, whose product is 1/6. Show the cancelling.
questions.a: Sample: 3/8 × 4/9. Cancel 3 with 9 by 3 and 4 with 8 by 4: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.
s: Gives two fractions with denominators 8 and 9
Shows the cancelling of common factors

questions.q: A water tank holds 2400 litres. After a night of rain it is 5/8 full. The school then uses 4/15 of the water in it for the garden. (a) How many litres are in the tank after the rain? (b) What fraction of the whole tank is used for the garden? (c) How many litres is that? Check it a second way using (a).
s: Part (c): 400 litres and the second route 4/15 × 1500 = 400

questions.q: Asha finds 18/35 × 25/54 by multiplying straight across; Bilal cancels first. (a) What are Asha's numerator and denominator before simplifying? (b) Simplify her fraction to lowest form. (c) Find Bilal's answer by cancelling 18 with 54 and 25 with 35. (d) Which method would you use for large numbers, and why?
questions.a: (a) 450/1890. (b) Dividing by 90 gives 5/21. (c) 1/3 × 5/7 = 5/21. (d) Cancelling first, since the numbers stay small and no big reduction is left; both give the same answer.
s: Part (c): 5/21 by cancelling 18 with 54 and 25 with 35
Part (d): picks a method with a reason about smaller numbers

questions.q: Ravi works out 3/8 × 5/12 by cancelling the denominators 8 and 12 by 4, getting 3/2 × 5/3 = 5/2. (a) What is wrong with his method? (b) Give the correct product.
questions.a: (a) He cancelled two denominators; only a numerator and a denominator can be cancelled. (b) 3/8 × 5/12 = 15/96 = 5/32.
s: Part (a): says two denominators cannot be cancelled together

questions.q: In the book, cancelling before multiplying means dividing by a common factor which two numbers?
questions.a: A numerator and a denominator, even from different fractions
o: A numerator and a denominator, even from different fractions
Two numerators that share a common factor, in different fractions
Two denominators that share a common factor, in different fractions
Only a numerator and a denominator that lie in the same fraction

questions.q:
A warehouse in Nashik can store 4200 quintal of onions and is now 5/6 full. Trader A offers ₹1,500 per quintal for 3/10 of the stored onions and pays at once. Trader B offers ₹1,800 per quintal for 2/7 of the stored onions but pays only after three months. The owner needs ₹15,00,000 in hand this week to buy seed for the next season and can sell to only one of them.
(a) How many quintal of onions are stored?
(b) How many quintal would each trader take?
(c) How much money would each trader pay?
(d) Which offer should the owner accept, and why? Use the money and the owner's need for cash.
questions.a: (a) 4200 × 5/6 = 3500 quintal. (b) A: 3/10 × 3500 = 1050; B: 2/7 × 3500 = 1000. (c) A: ₹15,75,000; B: ₹18,00,000. (d) A pays ₹15,75,000 today, which meets the ₹15,00,000 need; B pays ₹2,25,000 more but only after three months. Choosing A for the cash need, or B if the owner can find ₹15 lakh elsewhere, is acceptable when argued with these figures.
s: Part (d): decision weighing A's ₹15,75,000 today against B's extra ₹2,25,000 later

questions.q: What is 8/9 × 15/16 in lowest form?
To multiply the whole number 5 by 3/7 with Brahmagupta's formula, how is 5 written?
Find 7/8 × 5/6, then write 7/8, 5/6 and your product over the common denominator 48 to show the product is smaller than both factors.
questions.a: 7/8 × 5/6 = 35/48. With denominator 48: 7/8 = 42/48, 5/6 = 40/48 and 35/48 is less than both.

questions.q: (a) Find 3/7 × 14/9 and 14/9 × 3/7. (b) Which property of multiplication do your answers show?
questions.a: (a) Both equal 2/3. (b) The order of multiplication does not matter.
s: Part (b): states that order does not matter

questions.q: (a) Fill in: when one of the numbers multiplied is between 0 and 1, the product is ____ than the other number. (b) Use 2/3 × 12 to show this.
questions.a: (a) Less. (b) 2/3 × 12 = 8, which is less than 12.

questions.q: Show that two fractions each less than 1 cannot have the product 5/6 when one of them is 3/4.
questions.a: The product of two numbers between 0 and 1 is less than each of them, so the product would be less than 3/4. But 5/6 = 10/12 is more than 3/4 = 9/12, so it is impossible.
s: States the product is less than each factor

questions.q: Tina multiplies 20 by 5/4 and Rohit multiplies 20 by 3/4. Which statement is true?
questions.a: Tina's result is more than 20 and Rohit's is less than 20
o: Tina's result is more than 20 and Rohit's is less than 20
Both results are less than 20 because both multipliers are fractions
Both results are more than 20 because 20 is multiplied
Rohit's result is more than Tina's because 3/4 is the smaller multiplier

questions.q: A packet of 200 g sugar is repeatedly replaced by 9/10 of itself. (a) How much remains after the first step? (b) And after the second step? (c) What is the amount after the third step, as a fraction of a gram? (d) Will the amount ever become 0? Explain using what you know about multiplying by a number between 0 and 1.
questions.a: (a) 180 g. (b) 162 g. (c) 729/5 g. (d) No. Each step multiplies a positive amount by 9/10, which is between 0 and 1, so the new amount is smaller than the old one but is still a positive amount; it never reaches 0.
s: Part (d): never 0, because a positive amount multiplied by 9/10 stays positive and only gets smaller

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
Statement 1: The product 5/7 × 9/4 lies between 5/7 and 9/4.
Statement 2: Multiplying a number by a fraction always makes it smaller.
Statement 3: The order of multiplication never changes the product of two fractions.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q: Which statement about 2/9 × 4/5 and 4/5 × 2/9 is correct?
questions.a: They are equal because the order of multiplication does not matter
o: They are equal because the order of multiplication does not matter
The first is larger because the smaller fraction is multiplied first
The second is larger because the larger fraction is multiplied first
They are equal only when both of the fractions are below 1 in size

questions.q:
A dry-fruit shop in Hyderabad sells cashews at ₹100 per 100 g packet. In the Diwali week the shop multiplies the price by 6/5. After the festival the shop has 50 packets left and must clear them. Plan P multiplies the Diwali price by 4/5, and the owner expects to sell all 50 packets. Plan Q multiplies the Diwali price by 9/10, and the owner expects to sell only 40 packets now; the other 10 would be kept and sold next Diwali at the ₹120 price.
(a) What is the Diwali price of a packet?
(b) What is the clearance price under Plan P?
(c) Is the Plan P price more or less than the original ₹100? Explain using the product 6/5 × 4/5.
(d) Compare the total money from the two plans (including the 10 kept packets sold next year) and say which you would advise, giving one risk.
questions.a: (a) 100 × 6/5 = ₹120. (b) 120 × 4/5 = ₹96. (c) Less than ₹100, because 6/5 × 4/5 = 24/25 is less than 1. (d) Plan P: 50 × 96 = ₹4,800 at once. Plan Q: 40 × 108 = ₹4,320 plus 10 × 120 = ₹1,200 next year, ₹5,520 in all. Q brings ₹720 more but waits a year and the kept packets may not sell or may go stale; P is certain. Either choice is acceptable if argued with these figures.
s: Part (c): less than ₹100, since the combined multiplier 24/25 is below 1
Part (d): ₹4,800 against ₹5,520 and a decision naming a risk

questions.q: (a) Give a fraction f such that f × 6 is less than 6 but more than 3. (b) Give a fraction g such that g × 6 is more than 6. Show both products.
s: Part (a): a fraction between 1/2 and 1 with its product
Part (b): a fraction greater than 1 with its product

questions.q:
Eighteen litres of water fill a drum for the school's plant-watering relay. In the first round the Class 7A team pours 2/3 of the drum into a can. In the second round the Class 7B team pours a fraction of what is in the can onto the school plants, and whatever stays in the can goes to the Class 7C plants. The school plants need at least 10 1/4 litres and the Class 7C plants need at least 1 litre. The teacher is choosing the second fraction from 5/6, 7/8 and 11/12.
(a) How much water is in the can after the first round?
(b) How much reaches the school plants if the second fraction is 5/6, and is it enough?
(c) What fraction of the drum is that, and is it less than both 2/3 and 5/6?
(d) Which of 7/8 and 11/12 would you choose? Check what each leaves for both sets of plants.
questions.a: (a) 18 × 2/3 = 12 L. (b) 12 × 5/6 = 10 L, which is less than 10 1/4 L, so not enough. (c) 2/3 × 5/6 = 5/9 of the drum; it is less than both 2/3 and 5/6. (d) 7/8 gives the school plants 10 1/2 L and leaves 1 1/2 L for 7C: both enough with spare. 11/12 gives the school plants 11 L but leaves exactly 1 L for 7C: both enough, but 7C has no spare. Choosing 7/8 for spare on both sides, or 11/12 to favour the school plants, is acceptable when argued with these figures.
s: Part (c): 5/9 and says it is below both fractions
Part (d): checks 7/8 (10 1/2 and 1 1/2) and 11/12 (11 and 1) and decides

questions.q: When both numbers being multiplied are greater than 1, the product is
questions.a: greater than both the numbers

in between the two numbers multiplied

questions.q:

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Arun says, 'If I multiply 8 by a fraction between 0 and 1 the answer is smaller than 8, but if I multiply 8 by a fraction greater than 1 the answer is bigger than 8.' Is he right? Test with 3/4 and 7/4.
questions.a: Yes. 3/4 × 8 = 6, which is less than 8, and 7/4 × 8 = 14, which is greater than 8. The size of the product depends on whether the multiplier is below 1 or above 1.
s: Gives the verdict that Arun is right
States the rule in terms of the multiplier compared with 1

questions.q: Take the number 6/5 and multiply it by 4/9, by 1 and by 7/3. (a) Find the three products. (b) Compare each product with 6/5. (c) State in one sentence what decides whether the product is smaller than, equal to or bigger than 6/5.
questions.a: (a) 8/15, 6/5, 14/5. (b) 8/15 is less than 6/5, 6/5 is equal, 14/5 is greater. (c) It depends on whether the multiplier is below 1, equal to 1 or above 1.
s: Part (c): links the result to the multiplier compared with 1

questions.q: Anita makes 2/3 of a recipe that needs 2 1/2 cups of rice for the full recipe. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: She needs 1 2/3 cups, which is less than the full 2 1/2 cups
o: She needs 1 2/3 cups, which is less than the full 2 1/2 cups
She needs 3 3/4 cups, which is more than the full 2 1/2 cups
She needs 3 1/6 cups, which is more than the full 2 1/2 cups
She needs 1 2/3 cups, which is more than the full 2 1/2 cups

questions.q: Without multiplying, say whether each product is more than both, less than both, or between the two numbers: (a) 5/3 × 7/2 (b) 2/9 × 4/7 (c) 3/8 × 6.
questions.a: (a) More than both, since both exceed 1. (b) Less than both, since both are between 0 and 1. (c) Between 3/8 and 6, since one is below 1 and one is above 1.

questions.q: Without multiplying, decide whether 4/3 × 9/5 is more or less than 9/5 and give the reason; then check by finding the product.
questions.a: More than 9/5, because 4/3 is greater than 1. Check: 4/3 × 9/5 = 12/5, which is more than 9/5.
s: Says more with the reason that 4/3 is greater than 1
Finds 12/5 and confirms it is more than 9/5

questions.q: The product of 5/6 and 4 lies
questions.a: between 5/6 and 4

questions.q: Which pair of numbers gives a product that is less than both of them?
Half a kilogram of laddoos is shared equally among 6 children at the school fair. How much does each child get?
Gopal says 6 ÷ 2/3 = 4, since he wrote 6 × 2/3. Is he right? Say what he did wrong and check the correct answer with a multiplication.
questions.a: No. He multiplied by 2/3 instead of the reciprocal 3/2. 6 ÷ 2/3 = 6 × 3/2 = 9. Check: 2/3 × 9 = 6.
s: Gives the verdict that Gopal is wrong
Says he should multiply by the reciprocal 3/2 and gets 9

questions.q: (a) Write the reciprocals of 7/12 and of 9. (b) Show that a fraction multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1, using 7/12.

questions.a: reciprocal

questions.q: 3/5 litre of juice is poured equally into 6 glasses. (a) Write the division. (b) How much juice is in each glass?
What is 3/4 ÷ 5/8?

Situation A: a baker has 6 kg of flour and packs it in parcels of 3/4 kg. Situation B: a baker has 3/4 kg of flour and shares it equally among 6 cakes. (a) Write the division for each situation. (b) Find both answers with units. (c) Why do the two answers differ although the same numbers are used?
questions.a: (a) A: 6 ÷ 3/4. B: 3/4 ÷ 6. (b) A = 8 parcels. B = 1/8 kg per cake. (c) Division is not commutative: the total is the dividend and the size of one part is the divisor, so swapping them asks a different question.
s: Part (c): explains the dividend and divisor have different roles so order matters

questions.q: (a) Write 4/9 ÷ 2/7 as a missing-factor problem. (b) Solve it.
s: Part (b): multiplies 4/9 by the reciprocal 7/2 to get 14/9

questions.q: Three pumps fill the same tank. Pump 1 alone takes 1/2 hour, pump 2 takes 1/3 hour and pump 3 takes 1/6 hour. (a) How many tanks does each pump fill in 1 hour? (b) How many tanks do all three fill together in 1 hour? (c) How long do they take to fill one tank together, and is that less than the 1/6 hour of the fastest pump alone?
questions.a: (a) 1 ÷ 1/2 = 2, 1 ÷ 1/3 = 3, 1 ÷ 1/6 = 6. (b) 2 + 3 + 6 = 11 tanks. (c) 1/11 hour. Since 1/11 is less than 1/6, they are faster than the fastest pump alone.
s: Part (c): 1/11 hour and the comparison with 1/6 hour

questions.q: A tailor has a 3 m cloth strip and cuts pieces of 3/8 m each for pockets. How many pieces can he cut?
questions.a: 8 pieces

questions.q: What is 1 ÷ 3/7?

The art teacher at a school in Kolkata has 12 m of ribbon. A badge needs 3/8 m of ribbon and a medal needs 3/4 m. For prize day she wants 20 badges and 6 medals. Later the principal asks for 5 more badges. Ribbon is sold only in pieces of 2 m for ₹50 each.
(a) How many badges alone could 12 m make?
(b) How much ribbon do 20 badges and 6 medals need together?
(c) How much ribbon do the 5 extra badges need?
(d) Should she buy a 2 m piece, or tell the principal 5 extra badges are not possible? Give your reason.
questions.a: (a) 12 ÷ 3/8 = 32 badges. (b) 20 × 3/8 + 6 × 3/4 = 15/2 + 9/2 = 12 m, which is all her ribbon. (c) 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 m. (d) The 12 m is already used up, so she needs more ribbon. A 2 m piece for ₹50 covers 1 7/8 m with 1/8 m left, so buying it is sensible; a justified refusal on cost may also be accepted.
s: Part (d): decision using no ribbon left and 2 m covering 1 7/8 m

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 9/10 ÷ 3/5 = 3/2.

questions.q: (a) Find 5 ÷ 3/4. (b) Write the answer as a mixed fraction.
Write a real-life situation for 4 ÷ 1/3 and give its answer with a unit.
questions.a: Sample: A 4 m ribbon is cut into pieces of 1/3 m each. 4 ÷ 1/3 = 12 pieces.

questions.q:
A dairy in Anand has 7 1/2 litres of curd to pack. It can fill small cups of 3/20 litre, which sell at ₹12 each, or tubs of 3/4 litre, which sell at ₹55 each. All the curd goes into one kind of container only.
(a) How many cups can be filled?
(b) How many tubs can be filled?
(c) How much money does each choice bring?
(d) Which choice should the dairy make? Mention a point beyond the money.
questions.a: (a) 15/2 ÷ 3/20 = 50 cups. (b) 15/2 ÷ 3/4 = 10 tubs. (c) Cups 50 × 12 = ₹600; tubs 10 × 55 = ₹550. (d) Cups bring ₹50 more but need 50 containers to fill and seal against 10 for tubs, so more labour and packaging. Either choice is acceptable if justified with these figures.
s: Part (d): decision comparing ₹50 extra with 40 more containers

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
Statement 1: A fraction multiplied by its reciprocal always gives 1.
Statement 2: To divide by 4/5 we multiply by 5/4.
Statement 3: 1/6 ÷ 1/3 = 2.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q: A shopkeeper has 7/2 litres of coconut oil and fills bottles of 7/10 litre. (a) Write the division. (b) How many bottles does he fill? (c) Check your answer by multiplying.
A pipe 3 3/4 m long is cut into pieces of 1/4 m each. (a) Write 3 3/4 as an improper fraction. (b) How many pieces are cut?
(a) Without dividing, say whether 8 ÷ 2/3 is more or less than 8. (b) Find the quotient to check.
questions.a: (a) More, because the divisor 2/3 is between 0 and 1. (b) 8 × 3/2 = 12, which is more than 8.
s: Part (a): says more, with the reason about the divisor

questions.q: Sana says, 'Dividing 10 by a number greater than 1 gives something smaller than 10, and dividing 10 by a number between 0 and 1 gives something larger than 10.' Is she right? Test with 5/2 and 2/5.
questions.a: Yes. 10 ÷ 5/2 = 10 × 2/5 = 4, which is less than 10, and 10 ÷ 2/5 = 10 × 5/2 = 25, which is greater than 10. What matters is whether the divisor is above or below 1.
s: Gives the verdict that Sana is right
States the rule in terms of the divisor compared with 1

questions.q:
At the school fair, the canteen has 9 litres of lemon juice. It can sell cups of 1/5 litre at ₹6, cups of 1/3 litre at ₹9 or cups of 1/2 litre at ₹13. All the juice will be sold in one cup size. The volunteers can fill at most 30 cups before the fair closes.
(a) How many cups of each size can be filled from the 9 litres?
(b) Is each number more or less than 9, and why?
(c) How much money does each cup size bring?
(d) Which cup sizes are possible within the 30-cup limit, and which one earns most among them?
questions.a: (a) 45, 27 and 18 cups. (b) More than 9 each, since every cup size is a divisor between 0 and 1. (c) ₹270, ₹243 and ₹234. (d) The 1/5 litre cup needs 45 cups, above 30, so it is not possible. Of the other two, the 1/3 litre cup earns ₹243 and the 1/2 litre cup ₹234, so choose the 1/3 litre cup.
s: Part (b): more than 9, with the reason about divisors below 1
Part (d): rules out 45 cups and picks the 1/3 litre cup (₹243)

questions.q: A tailor says he can cut 12 scarves of 3/4 m each from 8 m of cloth. Show that this is impossible.
questions.a: 8 ÷ 3/4 = 8 × 4/3 = 32/3 = 10 2/3, so at most 10 whole scarves can be cut. Twelve scarves need 12 × 3/4 = 9 m, which is more than the 8 m available.

questions.a: greater than the dividend

questions.q: Mohan writes 4 ÷ 2/5 = 8/5. (a) Without working it out, explain why the answer must be more than 4. (b) Find the correct answer.

questions.q: A 4 m ribbon is cut into equal pieces. Find the number of pieces if each piece is (a) 1/2 m, (b) 1/4 m, (c) 1/8 m long. (d) Describe the pattern when the piece length is halved each time. (e) Predict the number of pieces of 1/16 m.
questions.a: (a) 8. (b) 16. (c) 32. (d) Each time the piece length is halved, the number of pieces doubles. (e) 64.

questions.q: The dividend stays 12. Which divisor gives the greatest quotient?
Is 9/10 ÷ 3 more or less than 9/10? Give the reason, and then find its value.
questions.a: Less, since the divisor 3 is greater than 1. Value: 9/10 × 1/3 = 3/10.

questions.q: The dividend is fixed at 6. (a) Find 6 ÷ 3/2, 6 ÷ 3/4 and 6 ÷ 3. (b) Compare each quotient with 6 and state the rule you see. (c) For which divisor is the quotient exactly 6? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 4, 8 and 2. (b) 4 and 2 are less than 6 (divisors 3/2 and 3 are above 1); 8 is more than 6 (divisor 3/4 is below 1). (c) A divisor of 1, since 6 ÷ 1 = 6.
s: Part (b): compares and states the rule on the divisor

questions.q:
A cloth merchant in Surat has 12 m of cloth. A scarf needs 3/4 m and sells for ₹120. A curtain needs 2 1/2 m and sells for ₹450. He compares two plans: Plan 1 makes scarves only; Plan 2 makes the greatest possible number of whole curtains first and then scarves from the cloth that is left.
(a) How many scarves can 12 m make under Plan 1?
(b) Under Plan 2, how many whole curtains can 12 m make, and how much cloth is left?
(c) How many whole scarves can the leftover make?
(d) Which plan earns more, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 12 ÷ 3/4 = 16 scarves. (b) 12 ÷ 5/2 = 4 4/5, so 4 curtains using 10 m, leaving 2 m. (c) 2 ÷ 3/4 = 2 2/3, so 2 whole scarves. (d) Plan 1: 16 × 120 = ₹1,920. Plan 2: 4 × 450 + 2 × 120 = ₹2,040. Plan 2 earns ₹120 more.

questions.a: 3 only

questions.q: In a word problem, '3/4 of 20 students' is calculated as
Ravi says, 'To find 1/2 of 1/3 of ₹600 I take one more fraction, so the answer must be more than 1/3 of ₹600.' Is he right? Work out both amounts.
questions.a: No. 1/3 of ₹600 = ₹200, and 1/2 of that is ₹100, which is less. Taking a fraction between 0 and 1 of an amount always gives less than the amount.

questions.q: A miser gives a beggar 1/3 of 1/4 of 1/5 of 3/2 dramma. A second miser gives 3/4 of 1/16 dramma. Take 1 dramma = 1280 cowrie shells. (a) What fraction of a dramma does the first miser give? (b) How many cowrie shells is that? (c) How many shells does the second miser give, and which beggar receives more?
questions.a: (a) 1/3 × 1/4 × 1/5 × 3/2 = 1/40 dramma. (b) 1280/40 = 32 shells. (c) 3/4 × 1/16 = 3/64 dramma = 60 shells. The second beggar receives more, by 28 shells.

questions.q: In the Līlāvatī problem, 1 dramma was equal to 1280 cowrie shells. How many cowrie shells is 1/8 of a dramma?
questions.a: 160 shells

questions.q: A floor area of 7/3 square units is to be covered with square bricks of side 1/3 unit. (a) Find the area of one brick. (b) How many bricks are needed?
questions.a: (a) 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9 square unit. (b) 7/3 ÷ 1/9 = 21 bricks.

questions.q:
Savita in Nagpur makes 4 1/2 kg of mango pickle and fills it into jars that hold 3/8 kg each. She sells 5/6 of the jars at ₹135 per jar. A neighbour offers to buy the remaining jars at 2/3 of the usual price, but Savita would have to spend ₹150 on an auto to deliver them. Otherwise she keeps the remaining jars for her family.
(a) How many jars does she fill?
(b) How many jars does she sell at ₹135 and how much does she receive?
(c) What is the discounted price per jar, and what do the remaining jars bring?
(d) After the ₹150 auto fare, how much does she gain by selling them, and how much pickle does she give up? Should she sell?
questions.a: (a) 9/2 ÷ 3/8 = 12 jars. (b) 5/6 × 12 = 10 jars, giving ₹1,350. (c) 2/3 × 135 = ₹90 per jar; the 2 remaining jars bring ₹180. (d) ₹180 - ₹150 = ₹30 gain, and she gives up 2 × 3/8 = 3/4 kg of pickle. Selling for ₹30 or keeping 3/4 kg for the family is acceptable when argued with these figures.
s: Part (c): ₹90 per jar and ₹180 for 2 jars
Part (d): ₹30 gain against 3/4 kg given up, with a decision

questions.q:
Class 7 raised ₹24,000 from its stall at the school mela. The class decided to spend 3/8 of the money on library books. Of the money that remained, 1/4 goes for a sports kit. The principal says that 2/5 of whatever is then left may be spent on a water cooler. The cooler the class likes costs ₹4,800.
(a) How much is spent on library books?
(b) How much is spent on the sports kit?
(c) How much is left after both, and how much may be spent on the cooler?
(d) What should the class do about the cooler? Give a reason using your numbers.
questions.a: (a) 3/8 × 24,000 = ₹9,000. (b) Remaining ₹15,000; 1/4 of it is ₹3,750. (c) ₹24,000 - 9,000 - 3,750 = ₹11,250 left; 2/5 of it is ₹4,500. (d) ₹4,500 is ₹300 less than ₹4,800. The class can add ₹300 from the other ₹6,750 left, or choose a cheaper cooler; any decision justified with these figures earns the mark.
s: Part (d): compares ₹4,500 with ₹4,800 and decides with a reason

questions.q: A bus has 40 seats and 3/5 of them are occupied. 1/4 of the people sitting are children. (a) How many seats are occupied? (b) How many children are on the bus?
Which ancient text, c. 800 BCE, contains the problem of covering an area with square bricks of fractional side?
questions.a: Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra

questions.q: Mira has a 360-page book. She reads 1/4 of it yesterday and 1/3 of it today. How many pages are left?
questions.a: 150 pages

questions.q: A farmer owns 1 acre of land. The government takes 1/5 of it for a canal, so 4/5 of the acre remains with her. Of the land that remains, she gives 3/8 to her nephew and 1/4 to her niece and keeps the rest. (a) What part of the original acre does the nephew get? (b) What part does the niece get? (c) What part does the farmer keep? Check that all four parts add up to 1 acre.
s: Part (c): 3/10 and the check that the parts total 1 acre

questions.q: A tank is 3/4 full. In the morning 2/3 of the water in it is used. (a) What fraction of the whole tank is used? (b) What fraction of the whole tank still has water?
Make up a word problem whose answer is 3/5 of 2/3 of 90 litres, and find the answer.
questions.a: Sample: A drum has 90 litres of water. 2/3 of it is poured into a tank and 3/5 of that is used for plants. Water used = 3/5 × 2/3 × 90 = 36 litres.

questions.q: A farmer has 4/5 acre of land. She gives 1/4 of it to her niece. How much land does the niece get?
questions.a: 1/5 acre

questions.q: A stationery wholesaler packs 12 pens in 1 box and 6 boxes in 1 carton. (a) What fraction of a carton is 1 pen? (b) What fraction of a carton is 9 pens?
questions.a: (a) 1 pen = 1/12 box and 1 box = 1/6 carton, so 1 pen = 1/12 × 1/6 = 1/72 carton. (b) 9 pens = 9/72 = 1/8 carton.
